context.concept_name: Retrieve resource

coverage.learning_objective: Retrieve a resource through the ORM: retrieve one resource by identity and test the not-found case.

required_facts.statement: Select mapped entities with await session.scalars(select(Entity).where(condition)) and inspect the resulting entity values rather than treating the result as an unbounded application-wide lookup.
Use await session.get(Entity, identity) for a primary-key lookup; it returns the identified entity or None when no row exists.
Add .limit(n) when selecting a bounded number of rows, and explicitly handle an empty result or None as absence.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A request wants a stored order, but a missing row is a valid lookup outcome to handle explicitly. Selection should match the intended identity or bounded condition.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Select mapped entities with await session.scalars(select(Entity).where(condition)) and inspect the resulting entity values rather than treating the result as an unbounded application-wide lookup.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Use await session.get(Entity, identity) for a primary-key lookup; it returns the identified entity or None when no row exists. Add .limit(n) when selecting a bounded number of rows, and explicitly handle an empty result or None as absence.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the retrieval form from the lookup requirement. If the request names a primary-key identity, get directly represents that lookup and has an explicit None outcome. If the requirement is a condition over several rows, select with where represents that condition and limit represents the intended bound. Inspect the resulting entities or empty result rather than assuming every successfully executed selection contains a match. The missing-row case belongs in the workflow before attribute use. This reasoning keeps retrieval precise: identify what is being selected, how many rows are intended, and what absence means for the next application step.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: For an identified order, await session.get(Order, identity) returns the entity or None. Trace both branches before using entity attributes. For a conditional selection, use session.scalars with select(Order).where(condition) and inspect the entity values. Add limit(n) when selecting a bounded number of rows. Compare one matching order, no matching orders and multiple matches under the bound. A result of None and an empty selection both represent absence in their respective lookup forms; neither should be treated as an existing entity. This exercise connects the lookup shape to the result handling rather than turning a selection into an unbounded application-wide search.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A successful lookup operation does not guarantee a row exists. Handle None or an empty result explicitly.

context.concept_name: Transaction commit and rollback boundaries

coverage.learning_objective: Choose transaction boundaries: implement one multi-write operation.

required_facts.statement: Use async with session.begin(): around related writes to commit on successful exit and roll back on exceptional exit.
A commit makes transaction changes durable, while a rollback discards uncommitted changes; multiple related writes belong in one transaction when they must succeed or fail together.
After a flush failure, explicitly roll back before reusing that session; a failed flush leaves its transactional state requiring recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Two related order writes must succeed or fail together. A transaction makes that joint boundary explicit rather than letting each write be treated as independently durable.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Use async with session.begin(): around related writes to commit on successful exit and roll back on exceptional exit.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A commit makes transaction changes durable, while a rollback discards uncommitted changes; multiple related writes belong in one transaction when they must succeed or fail together. After a flush failure, explicitly roll back before reusing that session; a failed flush leaves its transactional state requiring recovery.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Transaction recovery is observable separately from the original failure. In the two-write example, successful completion of the pair belongs to commit; exceptional exit belongs to rollback. A failed flush requires explicit rollback before session reuse even when application code has already caught the error. Therefore the recovery path should mention both the discarded uncommitted changes and the session state that must be recovered. Reporting only that an error was handled obscures whether either responsibility was met. Group the writes because the requirement ties their success together, and keep that requirement visible in the transaction scope.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Place related writes inside async with session.begin(). Successful exit commits; exceptional exit rolls back. Trace a first write followed by a failing second write: the exceptional transaction outcome should discard uncommitted changes rather than report a completed pair. Compare that with successful exit, which makes the changes durable. If a flush fails, explicitly roll back before reusing the session, because its transactional state requires recovery. Follow both data state and session state in the trace: a caught error message alone does not establish that either boundary has been recovered. The grouping should come from the requirement that the writes succeed or fail together, not merely from their proximity in the source file.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Catching a flush exception does not restore the session to usable transactional state. Roll back before reuse.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Choose transaction boundaries: implement one multi-write operation.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement one transaction boundary around two supplied asynchronous order-write helpers so that the writes succeed or fail together, without implementing their persistence details.
practice_anchor.success: Both helper calls run inside the same session.begin() scope. Successful exit commits the pair; an exception escaping the scope rolls back the uncommitted changes. A supplied standalone flush-failure recovery branch explicitly rolls back before session reuse.

live_code.required_skill: Group related asynchronous writes in one transaction and recover session state after a failed flush.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide an async operation with an idle session and two already-implemented order-write helpers. Leave the shared transaction scope unfinished. Separately provide a caught standalone flush-failure branch with a rollback placeholder before session reuse; learners do not implement write helpers or exception handling.
live_code.observable_success: The two supplied order writes share one transaction scope. A successful run makes both durable; a failure in the second helper leaves neither write committed. The standalone flush-failure branch awaits session.rollback() before the supplied session-reuse step.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the two order writes visible inside one transaction boundary, with successful exit leading to durable changes and exceptional exit leading to discarded uncommitted changes. Show a separate failed-flush recovery path requiring explicit rollback before session reuse.

teaching_notes: Establish this first: Related writes succeed or fail together.
Stay within the current objective: Choose transaction boundaries. Avoid extending the example into blocked later concepts.
Use the worked case to support this target: Determine commit and rollback effects.

context.concept_name: Bearer-token extraction into an authentication dependency

coverage.learning_objective: Extract bearer credentials from an API request: declare one bearer extraction dependency and verify absent and malformed credentials.

required_facts.statement: A bearer extraction dependency reads a credential from Authorization: Bearer token; receiving the credential does not itself establish that it is valid.
Declare Annotated[HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, Depends(HTTPBearer())] on a handler input and read its scheme and credentials fields to obtain the supplied bearer credential.
With HTTPBearer's default auto_error=True, absent credentials or a non-bearer scheme are rejected instead of supplied to the handler; verify absent and malformed Authorization headers separately.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A protected handler first needs to obtain a presented bearer credential. Extracting it is not the same as verifying that it is valid.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A bearer extraction dependency reads a credential from Authorization: Bearer token; receiving the credential does not itself establish that it is valid.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Declare Annotated[HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, Depends(HTTPBearer())] on a handler input and read its scheme and credentials fields to obtain the supplied bearer credential. With HTTPBearer's default auto_error=True, absent credentials or a non-bearer scheme are rejected instead of supplied to the handler; verify absent and malformed Authorization headers separately.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Declare Annotated[HTTPAuthorizationCredentials, Depends(HTTPBearer())] and read its scheme and credentials fields. A request with Authorization: Bearer followed by a supplied token presents the credential for later verification. With default auto_error=True, absent credentials and a non-bearer scheme are rejected instead of passed to the handler. Exercise absent and malformed Authorization headers separately so the extraction gate is visible. Then consider a presented bearer token: obtaining its text establishes only that extraction found a credential, not that its claims or authority are trustworthy. Keep that distinction in the trace so a handler does not mistake possession of a token-shaped value for completed authentication.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction

context.concept_name: Redis cache-aside selection and population

coverage.learning_objective: Implement cache-aside retrieval: add cache-aside retrieval to one read endpoint.

required_facts.statement: Cache-aside keeps a cache in front of a primary store; the primary store remains the source of truth rather than the cache becoming authoritative storage.
On a read, get the cache key first; on a miss, load from the primary store, cache the result and return it to the caller.
Cache-aside is useful for read-heavy data where repeated reads can reuse a copy and the application's staleness requirements permit that reuse.
Construct the cache key from the identity and parameters of the represented result so requests for different results do not reuse the wrong cached value.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: Repeated reads of an order may reuse a cached copy, but the database remains authoritative. Cache-aside separates accelerated reads from source-of-truth storage.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Cache-aside keeps a cache in front of a primary store; the primary store remains the source of truth rather than the cache becoming authoritative storage.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: On a read, get the cache key first; on a miss, load from the primary store, cache the result and return it to the caller. Cache-aside is useful for read-heavy data where repeated reads can reuse a copy and the application's staleness requirements permit that reuse. Construct the cache key from the identity and parameters of the represented result so requests for different results do not reuse the wrong cached value.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Trace a read for order 42. Check its cache key first. On a miss, load from the primary store, cache the result and return it. A later read may reuse that copy if the staleness requirements permit it. Choose the key from the identity and parameters of the represented result: order 43 or a differently parameterized result must not accidentally reuse order 42's value. Compare a hit and a miss in a two-path diagram, keeping both connected to the same represented result. Cache-aside is useful for read-heavy reuse, not a claim that any data can remain cached indefinitely. The cache is a disposable copy; the primary store is still the authority when deciding what the stored order actually is.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: A cache hit does not make the cache authoritative. A key must distinguish results whose identity or parameters differ.

video_need.reason: A drawn trace makes the distinct boundaries and direction of effects explicit rather than collapsing them into one step. Focus: Implement cache-aside retrieval: add cache-aside retrieval to one read endpoint.

media.group_title: Cache-aside: recover a miss and reuse a cached result

segments.label: Trace a Redis cache miss, population, and subsequent hit
segments.summary: The application checks Redis before querying the database. In the profile example, the first request finds no cached result: this is a cache miss. The application retrieves the profile from the database, stores a copy in Redis, and returns the response. A subsequent request finds that copy: this is a cache hit, so the application returns it without another database query. Reusing cached results can reduce database reads and improve response times; the speed claims illustrate the benefit rather than guarantee performance for every workload.

context.concept_name: Authoring, reviewing and applying Alembic schema migrations

coverage.learning_objective: Manage Alembic migrations: review one reversible migration.

required_facts.statement: Alembic maintains a migration environment and versioned revision scripts that describe schema changes through upgrade() and downgrade().
Generate a candidate revision with alembic revision --autogenerate -m "description", comparing the database schema with supplied target_metadata.
Autogeneration produces candidate changes that require manual review and correction; it does not reliably infer every schema intent such as table or column renames.
Apply revisions with alembic upgrade head and exercise alembic downgrade revision on a test database to verify a proposed reversal before using it operationally.
Review an autogenerated drop-and-add pair for a possible rename before applying it; dropping a column deletes the data stored in that column, so an apparent reversal may not recover that data.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A schema change needs a reviewed revision, not an assumption that automatic comparison understands every intended change.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Alembic maintains a migration environment and versioned revision scripts that describe schema changes through upgrade() and downgrade().

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Generate a candidate revision with alembic revision --autogenerate -m "description", comparing the database schema with supplied target_metadata. context.concept_name: Basic index selection for actual service queries

coverage.learning_objective: Select basic indexes: propose indexes for a small workload.

required_facts.statement: An index can speed up access to selected rows but adds overhead, so choose it for a query workload rather than indexing every column automatically.
PostgreSQL B-tree indexes support equality and ordered comparisons, making them candidates for frequently filtered or ordered values.
Propose CREATE INDEX name ON table (column) for a frequent lookup, accounting for extra storage and the cost of maintaining the index during writes.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A frequent order lookup may benefit from an index, but adding one changes storage and write costs too. Choose an access path for a workload, not for every available column.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: An index can speed up access to selected rows but adds overhead, so choose it for a query workload rather than indexing every column automatically.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: PostgreSQL B-tree indexes support equality and ordered comparisons, making them candidates for frequently filtered or ordered values. Propose CREATE INDEX name ON table (column) for a frequent lookup, accounting for extra storage and the cost of maintaining the index during writes.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Imagine frequent equality lookups on an external reference. A PostgreSQL B-tree index is a candidate because it supports equality and ordered comparisons. The supplied declaration form is CREATE INDEX name ON table (column). Propose that index for the frequent lookup while explicitly accounting for storage and maintenance during writes. Compare the benefit to the query workload with the added overhead; the fact that a column exists is not sufficient justification. For an ordered lookup, B-tree support makes it another candidate, not a guarantee of a particular performance gain. State the workload and the cost trade-off together so the recommendation is bounded by what this index is meant to help.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: An index can speed selected-row access but adds overhead. Do not turn that possibility into a guarantee or index every column automatically.

context.concept_name: Keeping API schemas distinct from persistence entities

coverage.learning_objective: Separate API and ORM models: define public schemas around one entity.

required_facts.statement: A persistence model maps stored rows, while a public response model declares the fields clients receive; these are separate contracts even when they describe the same entity.
Define separate public input and output BaseModel classes and use response_model=PublicOutput to prevent persistence-only or sensitive fields from automatically becoming API fields.

Use model_config = ConfigDict(from_attributes=True) when a Pydantic public model should validate values from an object's attributes, rather than requiring its persistence class to be the public schema.

teaching_blocks.content: An order row and the JSON contract may describe the same entity while exposing different fields. Persistence and public API models have different responsibilities.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: A persistence model maps stored rows, while a public response model declares the fields clients receive; these are separate contracts even when they describe the same entity.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: Define separate public input and output BaseModel classes and use response_model=PublicOutput to prevent persistence-only or sensitive fields from automatically becoming API fields. context.concept_name: Translating domain and persistence failures at the API boundary

coverage.learning_objective: Translate internal failures at the API boundary: translate one storage conflict into a stable API error.

required_facts.statement: Register @app.exception_handler(FailureClass) to translate a recognized internal failure into an intentional public HTTP response.
A write conflicting with an existing uniqueness rule can be represented as 409 when that is the API's declared conflict outcome, instead of exposing database exception text.
Recover a failed persistence transaction with rollback and translate the recognized failure at the API boundary rather than treating the failed session as usable or disclosing its internals.

teaching_blocks.title: The situation
teaching_blocks.content: A recognized uniqueness conflict should become the API's declared public outcome, not a leak of database exception text.

teaching_blocks.title: The rule and its boundary
teaching_blocks.content: Register @app.exception_handler(FailureClass) to translate a recognized internal failure into an intentional public HTTP response.

teaching_blocks.title: How to use the rule
teaching_blocks.content: A write conflicting with an existing uniqueness rule can be represented as 409 when that is the API's declared conflict outcome, instead of exposing database exception text. Recover a failed persistence transaction with rollback and translate the recognized failure at the API boundary rather than treating the failed session as usable or disclosing its internals.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Register an exception handler for a recognized FailureClass at the API boundary. For a uniqueness conflict whose contract declares 409, translate the recognized failure to that outcome. If persistence has failed, roll back the transaction before further session use. Trace the failure through two responsibilities: recovery restores the persistence boundary, while translation expresses the public HTTP meaning. Merely translating the exception does not prove the session recovered, and merely rolling back does not specify what the client receives. Keep the public response intentional and avoid exposing database internals. The declared conflict mapping applies to a recognized case, not to every exception that happens during a write.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Do not map every database failure to conflict or treat a failed session as usable because an HTTP response was produced.

required_facts.statement: JWT decoding without verification reveals claims but does not establish that the claims are trustworthy.

Expiration and not-before claims constrain token time validity; checks for a claim's value are distinct from requiring that the claim be present. Treat a library verification exception as an invalid credential and reject the protected request rather than using its unverified claims.

teaching_blocks.title: Why the distinction matters
teaching_blocks.content: Keep three columns in the token review: readable claim, required claim and verified claim value. Opening a token without verification fills only the first kind of observation. The verifier must use trusted algorithm and key configuration, require the intended claims, and check their values under issuer, audience and time policy. Expiration and not-before constrain validity, but a value check and a presence requirement are not interchangeable. If the library rejects verification, the protected request must reject the credential rather than reuse the readable payload. That final rejection branch is part of the trust boundary, not an optional diagnostic detail.

teaching_blocks.title: Reason through an example
teaching_blocks.content: Choose the allowed algorithm, key, issuer and audience from trusted configuration, not the token alone. Decode with verification and explicitly require exp, iss and aud. Requiring a claim and checking its value are distinct: a time check is not the same as guaranteeing the claim is present. Expiration and not-before constrain time validity. Trace a token through verification, then trusted context; a library verification exception should lead to credential rejection rather than fallback use of unverified claims. Compare a token merely opened for inspection with one accepted under all configured checks. The readable payload in the first case is information, not evidence that the caller is entitled to use its asserted identity or permissions.

teaching_blocks.title: Keep this distinction
teaching_blocks.content: Decoding without verification is not authentication. The token itself must not choose the allowed algorithm.

segments.label: How expiry and write invalidation trigger a fresh read
segments.summary: A cached project list becomes stale when a new project is added to the database without changing the cached copy.
